title: Finite entropy sums in quantum field theory: the Fourier-coefficient criterion for safe functions on a hypergraph (Lemma 4.2)
author: Mark Van Raamsdonk
work: Finite entropy sums in quantum field theory
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the paper's Fourier-coefficient criterion for the safe functions on a hypergraph, printed as Lemma 4.2 (source0.tex lines 557--560), delivered together with the paper's complete original proof of it at source0.tex lines 571--621. The preparation note for this item paired that fifty-one-line proof block with the theorem that follows the lemma, and it is worth correcting, because the block's own first line is a proof environment carrying the annotation (Lemma FourLemma) and FourLemma is the label of the lemma at source0.tex line 558. The theorem printed immediately after the lemma, Theorem 4.3, has no proof of its own: the paper says only that it follows by the same logic as the proof of its earlier graph-theoretic Fourier theorem. The counted unit is therefore the lemma, and the fifty-one-line block is the paper's own complete proof of it. The proof is a self-contained Boolean-cube argument. It fixes an intersection I and a bipartition of I, writes the safety condition (13) in the Fourier basis as the vanishing of a sum against the test function g of the bipartition (14), and computes the inner product of g with each Fourier character. For any vertex outside I the contributing sets come in complementary pairs obtained by toggling that vertex, and the two terms cancel whenever the vertex lies in the character's index set, so the inner product can be nonzero only for index sets contained in I; on those sets the contributing terms are exactly the sets of the form a union phi and b union phi with phi disjoint from I, and after factoring out the common characters the sum evaluates to a two-term expression whose bracket vanishes exactly when the parity conditions on a and b agree with the index set. That reduces the whole safety condition to the system (15) over even-order subsets of I. The paper then counts the system: one equation per bipartition, that is one fewer than the number of unknowns, and it proves independence rather than assuming it. Fixing a distinguished element of I, parametrising bipartitions by the nonempty subsets of the remaining set, and introducing the bijection that turns an arbitrary subset into an even-order subset by adjoining the distinguished element when the order is odd, it rewrites the system as the vanishing of a function on the remaining Boolean cube against every nonempty point (16), and concludes from the invertibility of the Fourier basis there that all the coefficients attached to even-order subsets of I are equal. That is precisely the statement. The argument is not an exercise: it requires the cancellation-by-complementary-pairs step, the parity reduction, and the change of variables that turns the system into a Fourier-invertibility statement, and none of these is a routine verification of a definition. It is the paper's own technical core, its result is what the theorem printed immediately after it is deduced from, and no qualifying examination poses it, which places it in the upper qualifying-to-research range: H2.
